title: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
summary: How a BPF program decides which thread runs where: the EEVDF baseline, dispatch queues and callbacks, weighted vtime, building a scheduler, placement, custody, safety and measurement.
outcomes: Explain where the ext scheduling class sits among the kernel's classes and which tasks it takes over
Run EEVDF's eligibility and virtual-deadline rules on numbers and name what fair-class knobs cannot express
Trace a task through select_cpu, enqueue, dispatch, dequeue and the local, global and custom dispatch queues
Predict CPU shares under scx_simple, including the 50 percent cap caused by dispatch running before re-enqueue
Build, load and extend a scheduler with libbpf, task storage and exit info, and read why it was unloaded
Use idle tracking, kicks, LOCAL_ON and per-LLC queues to control where and when tasks run
Explain how the verifier, callback checks, the watchdog and SysRq-S return a machine to the fair class
Benchmark a scheduler against EEVDF with latency percentiles and check which nice and cgroup controls it honors

lessons.title: Why the kernel lets a BPF program pick the next thread

blocks.md: Every time a CPU finishes or preempts a thread, the kernel scheduler answers one question: which runnable thread goes next, on which CPU, for how long. On Linux that answer for ordinary threads comes from the fair class (CFS, now EEVDF), one general-purpose policy compiled into the kernel for every workload on every machine. CFS, the Completely Fair Scheduler (Linux 2.6.23, 2007), gives every thread a *virtual runtime* (vruntime): the CPU time it has used, scaled down for threads with a larger weight. It always runs the thread with the smallest vruntime, so over time each thread gets CPU in proportion to its weight. Linux 6.6 replaced that pick rule with EEVDF, Earliest Eligible Virtual Deadline First: among threads that have not yet received more than their fair share (the eligible ones), it runs the one whose virtual deadline, its virtual start time plus its requested slice scaled by its weight, comes first. A thread's weight comes from its *nice* value, from -20 (most CPU) to 19 (least), with 0 as the default.

General purpose is the problem. A game wants low tail latency for its render thread, a VM host wants long uninterrupted runs for vCPUs (virtual CPUs: host threads that each run one guest processor), a server fleet wants a latency-critical service protected from batch jobs. Tuning knobs only go so far, and the policy itself is fixed.

The naive fix is to patch the scheduler. The sched_ext authors list why that is slow: the scheduler codebase takes newcomers a long time to learn, and every experiment means rebuild the kernel, reboot, rewarm the workload (they cite hours to warm memcache, Meta's in-memory key-value cache,) and rerun. Rolling a new kernel across a fleet can take months. A bug in a patched scheduler can crash the machine.

**sched_ext** (the extensible scheduler class, merged in Linux 6.12) changes the deal: the policy is a set of BPF programs, loaded by running a user-space binary and removed by stopping it, with the kernel guaranteeing it can always fall back to the fair class.

Recall from the prerequisite courses: a *thread* (task) is the unit the scheduler places on a CPU, and BPF programs are verified and JIT-compiled before the kernel runs them. sched_ext uses a BPF feature called **struct_ops**: user space loads a table of BPF functions that fill in a kernel-defined struct of callbacks, here `struct sched_ext_ops`. The only mandatory field is `.name`; every callback is optional and has a default. The figure below shows how that table gets from a user-space binary into the kernel.

The kernel keeps several *scheduling classes* in strict priority order. On each pick it asks the highest class that has a runnable task.

blocks.title: How a struct of BPF programs becomes the scheduler

scenes.caption: The binary (say scx_simple) opens its BPF object and loads every callback as its own BPF program. The verifier checks each one and the JIT compiles it, as for any BPF program.
Each program goes into one slot of a struct_ops map whose type is the kernel's struct sched_ext_ops, next to the name and flags. SCX_OPS_DEFINE puts that struct in the .struct_ops.link section.
Attaching the map (bpf_map__attach_struct_ops) creates a BPF link. Registering it runs the scheduler's init callback, then moves tasks to the ext class.
From now on every scheduling event calls through the table: the core invokes this map's select_cpu, enqueue, dispatch and the rest.
Destroying the link (the binary exits or calls bpf_link__destroy) unregisters the table. The exit reason reads "unregistered from user space" and every task returns to fair.

blocks.md: Which class a thread belongs to follows from its *scheduling policy*, set with the `sched_setscheduler()` system call: `SCHED_NORMAL` (the default), `SCHED_BATCH` and `SCHED_IDLE` belong to the fair class, `SCHED_FIFO` and `SCHED_RR` to realtime, `SCHED_DEADLINE` to deadline, and sched_ext adds a new policy, `SCHED_EXT`. One more term for the diagram: SysRq is the kernel's emergency key handler (the SysRq key plus a letter, or a letter written to `/proc/sysrq-trigger`), which the kernel processes even when user space is unresponsive.

blocks.title: Where sched_ext sits among the scheduling classes

scenes.caption: Classes are asked in this order on every pick. With no BPF scheduler loaded, the ext class is skipped and even tasks that set SCHED_EXT are run by the fair class as if they were SCHED_NORMAL.
A scheduler binary loads its sched_ext_ops. Without the SCX_OPS_SWITCH_PARTIAL flag, every SCHED_NORMAL, BATCH, IDLE and EXT task moves to sched_ext and the fair class is skipped entirely.
With SCX_OPS_SWITCH_PARTIAL set, only tasks that chose SCHED_EXT go to the BPF scheduler. The rest stay in fair, which sits above ext, so a runnable fair task always wins the CPU.

On an error, a stalled runnable task, SysRq-S, or the binary exiting, the kernel unloads the BPF scheduler and moves every task back to the fair class. Realtime and deadline tasks were never affected.

blocks.code:
# kernel built with CONFIG_SCHED_CLASS_EXT=y, BPF, BPF_JIT, DEBUG_INFO_BTF
cat /sys/kernel/sched_ext/state      # prints: disabled
sudo scx_simple &                    # load: runs the BPF scheduler
cat /sys/kernel/sched_ext/state      # prints: enabled
cat /sys/kernel/sched_ext/root/ops   # prints: simple
grep ext /proc/self/sched            # ext.enabled : 1
kill %1                              # unload: everyone returns to fair
blocks.caption: Switching a whole machine to a BPF scheduler and back, following the kernel docs. No reboot, no kernel rebuild.

blocks.md: sched_ext does not replace the scheduler core. It is one more scheduling class, below fair and above idle, whose *policy* (which task, which CPU, how long) is delegated to BPF callbacks while the core keeps the mechanism (run queues, context switches, preemption by higher classes).

Misconception: loading a BPF scheduler lets you control realtime or deadline threads. It cannot. Stop, deadline and realtime classes sit above ext and preempt it; sched_ext only takes over tasks that would otherwise be in the fair class.

blocks.question: A BPF scheduler is loaded with SCX_OPS_SWITCH_PARTIAL. On one CPU, a SCHED_NORMAL thread and a SCHED_EXT thread are both runnable. Which runs first?
options: The SCHED_EXT thread, because the BPF scheduler has been loaded and owns that CPU
The SCHED_NORMAL thread, because the fair class has higher precedence than ext
Whichever has the smaller virtual runtime, compared across both classes
Neither: mixing classes on one CPU makes the kernel abort the BPF scheduler
blocks.explain: Classes are consulted in strict order: stop, deadline, realtime, fair, ext, idle. In partial mode the fair class is still active and sits above ext, so its runnable task is picked first. Vruntime is never compared across classes.

blocks.question: Which problem does sched_ext mainly remove compared with patching CFS directly?
options: Scheduling decisions must be made in user space, which adds a context switch per pick
BPF programs run faster than compiled kernel C, so a fixed policy becomes cheaper
Each policy change needs a kernel rebuild, reboot, workload rewarm and fleet rollout, and a bug can crash the host
The fair class cannot run on machines with more than one L3 cache
blocks.explain: The motivation is iteration speed and safety: a policy is loaded and unloaded like a program, and the kernel can always revert to fair. BPF schedulers mostly run in the kernel (user space involvement is optional), and BPF is not faster than native kernel code.

lessons.title: The baseline you replace: EEVDF picks and the knobs it offers

blocks.md:
Before replacing a scheduler, know exactly what it does. Recall from the prerequisite course on processes and threads: the fair class charges *vruntime* $\Delta v = \Delta t \times 1024/w$, nice sets the weight $w$ (nice 0 is 1024, nice 5 is 335), and EEVDF runs, among *eligible* tasks, the one with the earliest *virtual deadline*. The default requested slice is 0.7 ms x (1 + ilog2(min(CPUs, 8))), where ilog2 is the base-2 logarithm rounded down: 2.8 ms on 8 or more CPUs.

That course gave the definitions. This lesson runs them on numbers, because later lessons compare BPF schedulers with exactly this behavior: scx_bpfland is modeled on it and scx_lavd builds its own deadlines.

The precise rules, from the kernel's EEVDF document and `kernel/sched/fair.c`:

- $V$ is the weighted average vruntime of the runnable tasks (the kernel's `avg_vruntime()`).
- A task's **lag** is the service it is owed: what it should have received minus what it got, which works out to $w_i(V - v_i)$. The name says it: the task lags behind its fair share.
- A task is **eligible** when its lag is zero or more, that is when $v_i \le V$.
- Its **virtual deadline** is its vruntime plus its requested slice $r_i$ in virtual time. When it has used that slice, the deadline moves one slice further.

blocks.caption: EEVDF in two formulas: only tasks at or behind the weighted average may run, and among them the earliest virtual deadline wins.

blocks.md:
A tiny example. Two CPU-bound tasks share one CPU, both at nice 0 ($w = 1024$, so virtual time equals real time). Task A requests a 3 ms slice; task B requests 1 ms with `sched_setattr()` (its `sched_runtime` field; the kernel clamps a custom slice to 0.1 to 100 ms). Both start at $v = 0$.

Simplified model: once picked, a task runs until it reaches its deadline, and picks happen only then. The kernel also re-checks on ticks and on wakeups.

blocks.title: EEVDF on one CPU: a 3 ms request (A) and a 1 ms request (B)

scenes.caption: t = 0: both are eligible (v = V = 0). Deadlines: A 0 + 3 = 3, B 0 + 1 = 1. B's is earlier, so B runs first.
t = 1: B has v = 1 while V = 0.5, so B is ahead of the average and not eligible. A (v = 0) is, and runs to its deadline at v = 3.
t = 4: V = 2. B (v = 1, deadline 2) is eligible and beats A's new deadline 6. B runs three 1 ms pieces until its v = 4 passes V = 3.5.
The pattern repeats every 6 ms: 3 ms of A, three 1 ms pieces of B. Each gets 50 percent of the CPU; B got the CPU first and never waits more than one 3 ms run of A.

blocks.prompt: Now B requests 0.5 ms instead of 1 ms, everything else unchanged. Does B's long-run CPU share change?
blocks.reveal: No. Running the same model with $r_B = 0.5$ ms still gives exactly 50 percent each. Eligibility ties every task to the weighted average $V$: B can only run while $v_B \le V$, so with equal weights neither task can pull ahead for long. A shorter request changes *when* and *in how many pieces* B runs, not *how much*. To change the share you change the weight, with nice or the `cpu.weight` of the task's cgroup (control group: the kernel's way to give a group of processes a CPU share or limit, as containers use).

blocks.md:
Those are the knobs the fair class offers, and each one feeds a number into the same fixed rule:

- **nice** (-20 to 19): the weight, so the share.
- **`sched_setattr()` slice** (0.1 to 100 ms): how early a task's deadline falls and how long it runs at once.
- **policy**: `SCHED_BATCH`, or `SCHED_IDLE` for leftover CPU.
- **cgroup** `cpu.weight` (1 to 10000, default 100), `cpu.max` (a quota per period) and `cpu.idle`.
- **affinity** (`sched_setaffinity()`): which CPUs a task may use.

What no knob says is a different *rule*. The sched_ext authors list such cases in the scx overview: VM scheduling, where a fixed set of long-running vCPUs allows optimizations the overview calls infeasible in CFS, such as long uninterrupted runs; acting on hints straight from the application, such as a service that knows the deadline of each incoming RPC; and central scheduling, where one CPU makes every decision so the others run undisturbed. Those need code, not parameters, and that is the gap sched_ext fills.

EEVDF in one line: weight sets the share, the requested slice sets the latency, and eligibility keeps any task from running far ahead of its share. A BPF scheduler gets none of this for free; lesson 5 shows the minimal one getting weights only partly right.
Misconception: a shorter slice buys a task more CPU. Under EEVDF it buys an earlier deadline and more, shorter turns; the total still follows the weights.

blocks.question: Two CPU-bound tasks at the same nice share one CPU under EEVDF. X requests a 0.5 ms slice, Y requests 4 ms. What share does X get in the long run?
options: About 89 percent, since 4 / (4 + 0.5) of the deadlines favor X
About 11 percent, since X asks for so little each time
About 50 percent: equal weights, X just runs in shorter, more frequent pieces
It depends on HZ, because slices end on ticks
blocks.explain: Share follows weight. Eligibility ($v_i \le V$) stops X from running ahead of the average however early its deadlines are. The short request only makes X run sooner and in smaller pieces.

blocks.question: Which of these needs a new scheduling rule (sched_ext) rather than a fair-class knob?
options: Pick the next thread using the deadline that the application attached to each RPC
Give a backup job about a quarter of the CPU a build gets
Let a latency-sensitive thread run in 0.5 ms pieces
Cap a container at 1.5 CPUs
blocks.explain: Nice handles the share, `sched_setattr()` the slice, and `cpu.max` the cap. Ordering work by a deadline the application knows is a different rule, one of the motivating cases in the scx overview.

lessons.title: Dispatch queues: how tasks travel from BPF to a CPU

blocks.md:
The scheduler core works per CPU: each CPU picks from its own run queue under its own lock. A BPF scheduler may want something else entirely: one global queue, one queue per L3 cache (the last-level cache that a group of cores shares, lesson 7), a priority queue per cgroup (a *control group*: the kernel's way to put processes in a group and give the group a CPU share or limit, as containers do). sched_ext bridges the two with **dispatch queues (DSQs)**.

A DSQ is a queue of tasks that can behave as a FIFO or, for DSQs the scheduler creates, as a priority queue ordered by a 64-bit *vtime* value. vtime, short for virtual time, is a number the BPF scheduler assigns to each task, and the smallest is served first; lesson 5 shows how `scx_simple` computes it from the CPU time a task used and its weight. Three kinds exist:

- one **local DSQ** per CPU (`SCX_DSQ_LOCAL`): the only place a CPU ever runs a task from,
- one **global DSQ** (`SCX_DSQ_GLOBAL`), a FIFO shared by all CPUs,
- any number of **custom DSQs** created with `scx_bpf_create_dsq()`.

Vocabulary from the kernel docs: a task is **inserted** into a DSQ (`scx_bpf_dsq_insert()` for FIFO order, `scx_bpf_dsq_insert_vtime()` for priority order), and a task sitting in a non-local DSQ is **moved** to a CPU's local DSQ (`scx_bpf_dsq_move_to_local()`). Linux 6.12 called these `scx_bpf_dispatch()` and `scx_bpf_consume()`; the names changed later, which is typical: sched_ext gives no API stability promise to BPF schedulers.

When a CPU needs its next task, the rule is fixed: take the head of its local DSQ; if empty, move one from the global DSQ; if that is empty too, call the BPF scheduler's `ops.dispatch()` and let it fill the local DSQ.

blocks.title: Two CPUs picking work from local, global and custom DSQs

scenes.caption: Starting state. CPU0 has two tasks in its local DSQ. The BPF scheduler has inserted T3, T4, T5 into custom DSQ 0 (created with scx_bpf_create_dsq). CPU1 has just gone free.
CPU1 looks at its local DSQ (empty), then the global DSQ (empty). Only now does the core call ops.dispatch(cpu=1) on the BPF scheduler.
ops.dispatch calls scx_bpf_dsq_move_to_local(0). T3 moves from custom DSQ 0 into CPU1's local DSQ, and CPU1 runs it.
A new task T6 wakes up and the scheduler's ops.enqueue inserts it into SCX_DSQ_GLOBAL, the built-in shared FIFO.
CPU1 is free again. Its local DSQ is empty, so it takes T6 from the global DSQ. ops.dispatch is not called, so T4 keeps waiting even though it has been queued longer.
CPU0 always drains its own local DSQ first: T1 runs, then T2, before CPU0 would ever look at global or custom DSQs. Whatever lands in a local DSQ is committed to that CPU.

blocks.prompt: A scheduler only ever calls scx_bpf_dsq_insert() with SCX_DSQ_GLOBAL or SCX_DSQ_LOCAL from its enqueue callback. Does it need an ops.dispatch() callback at all?
blocks.reveal: No. Tasks never wait inside the BPF scheduler: they are already in the global or a local DSQ, and the core consumes both automatically before it would call `ops.dispatch()`. The kernel docs say exactly this, and the default `ops.enqueue()` (insert into `SCX_DSQ_GLOBAL`) is why a scheduler with only a name already works. You need `ops.dispatch()` once you park tasks in custom DSQs or in BPF maps.

blocks.md: DSQ ids are 64-bit values. Bit 63 (`SCX_DSQ_FLAG_BUILTIN`) marks the built-in queues, so custom DSQ ids must be below $2^{63}$. Bit 62 marks `SCX_DSQ_LOCAL_ON`, and the low 32 bits then carry a CPU number, which lets a scheduler running on one CPU insert straight into another CPU's local DSQ. Values computed from `include/linux/sched/ext.h`:

blocks.code:
SCX_DSQ_FLAG_BUILTIN = 1 << 63
SCX_DSQ_FLAG_LOCAL_ON = 1 << 62
SCX_DSQ_GLOBAL   = BUILTIN | 1         = 0x8000000000000001
SCX_DSQ_LOCAL    = BUILTIN | 2         = 0x8000000000000002
SCX_DSQ_LOCAL_ON | 3 (CPU 3's local)   = 0xc000000000000003
largest custom DSQ id = 2^63 - 1        = 0x7fffffffffffffff
blocks.caption: DSQ id layout. Custom ids such as 0 used by scx_simple never collide with built-in ones.

blocks.md: The two built-in DSQ types are FIFOs only. To order tasks by vtime you must create a custom DSQ and use `scx_bpf_dsq_insert_vtime()` on it; the kernel rejects vtime insertion into `SCX_DSQ_LOCAL` or `SCX_DSQ_GLOBAL`. This is why `scx_simple` creates DSQ 0 in its `init` callback instead of using the global DSQ.
A CPU only ever runs tasks from its own local DSQ. Everything else (global DSQ, custom DSQs, BPF maps) is staging. The pick order is local, then global, then `ops.dispatch()`.

Inserting a task into a local DSQ is a commitment. Once there, it waits for that CPU even if another CPU goes idle a microsecond later. Schedulers that want work sharing keep tasks in a shared custom DSQ and move them to a local DSQ only when a CPU asks via `ops.dispatch()`.

blocks.question: CPU2's local DSQ is empty. The global DSQ holds task X (queued 1 ms ago) and custom DSQ 7 holds task Y (queued 50 ms ago). Which task does CPU2 run next, assuming no new insertions?
options: Y, because it has waited longer and DSQs are served oldest first across queues
X, because the global DSQ is consumed before ops.dispatch() is ever called
Y, because custom DSQs have priority over built-in ones
Neither until ops.dispatch() chooses between them
blocks.explain: The pick order is fixed: local DSQ, then global DSQ, then ops.dispatch(). X is taken from the global DSQ without consulting the BPF scheduler. Y only moves if ops.dispatch() later calls scx_bpf_dsq_move_to_local(7).

blocks.question: Your enqueue callback calls scx_bpf_dsq_insert_vtime(p, SCX_DSQ_GLOBAL, slice, vtime, flags). What happens?
options: Tasks are kept in vtime order inside the global DSQ
The vtime is ignored and the task is appended FIFO
It is an error: built-in DSQs do not support priority-queue insertion, so you need a custom DSQ
The task is silently moved to the caller CPU's local DSQ
blocks.explain: Built-in DSQs (local and global) are FIFO only. The docs and scx_simple's comments say vtime insertion needs a DSQ created with scx_bpf_create_dsq(); invalid use is reported as a scheduler error, which unloads it.

lessons.title: The scheduling cycle: select_cpu, enqueue, dispatch, run

blocks.md:
A BPF scheduler is a set of callbacks the core invokes at specific moments in a task's life. The ones that make decisions for a waking task are:

1. `ops.select_cpu(p, prev_cpu, wake_flags)`: pick a CPU for a waking task. It is a *hint*, and choosing an idle CPU also wakes that CPU up.
2. `ops.enqueue(p, enq_flags)`: the task is runnable; insert it into a DSQ or keep it in BPF data structures (a map, a list).
3. `ops.dispatch(cpu, prev)`: a CPU has nothing in its local or the global DSQ; fill its local DSQ.

Around them sit notification callbacks: `runnable`, `running` (task starts on a CPU), `tick` (every 1/HZ while running), `stopping` (task leaves the CPU), `quiescent` (task stops being runnable), plus per-task `init_task`, `enable`, `disable`, `exit_task`. HZ is the kernel's timer interrupt rate, fixed at build time by `CONFIG_HZ` (commonly 250 or 1000 per second), so the tick comes every 4 ms or 1 ms; one tick interval is called a *jiffy*.

Each insertion carries a **slice**, the time budget in nanoseconds the task may run before the core asks the scheduler again. The kernel's default `SCX_SLICE_DFL` is 20 ms. While the task runs, the core decrements `p->scx.slice`; at zero the task is descheduled. If a scheduler forgets to set a slice, the core refills it with `SCX_SLICE_DFL` and counts it in the `SCX_EV_REFILL_SLICE_DFL` event.

Here is a waking task on a busy machine, following `scx_simple`, the kernel's minimal example scheduler that keeps every task in one shared vtime-ordered custom DSQ. `scx_simple` also keeps one global number, `vtime_now`: whenever a task starts running, `vtime_now` moves up to that task's vtime if it is larger, so it tracks how far virtual time has advanced. When a task stops, `scx_simple` charges its vtime for the time used, scaled down for heavier tasks (formula in lesson 5): busy tasks drift forward, a sleeper falls behind. So a waking task more than one slice behind `vtime_now` is raised to `vtime_now` minus one slice, and a long sleep cannot bank unlimited priority.

blocks.title: When each notification callback fires for one task

scenes.caption: t = 0: p wakes while q holds the only free CPU. select_cpu() returns a hint, then runnable() (p is now runnable) and enqueue() put p in a DSQ, where it waits.
t = 6 ms: q blocks. The CPU's dispatch() moves p to its local DSQ and running(p) fires. While p runs, tick(p) fires every 1/HZ (4 ms at HZ = 250) and its 20 ms slice counts down.

t = 26 ms: the slice is used up. The CPU's dispatch(prev = p) runs first and takes q; only then stopping(p, runnable = true) charges p and enqueue() queues it again. p stayed runnable, so no quiescent().

t = 36 ms: q blocks, dispatch() and running(p) again. At 48 ms p blocks in read() with 8 ms of slice left: stopping(p, runnable = false), then quiescent(p). When the read completes, the cycle restarts at runnable().

blocks.title: One wakeup through scx_simple when no CPU is idle

scenes.caption: Task p wakes. The core first asks select_cpu. The default helper finds no idle CPU, so the callback just returns a hint and inserts nothing.
Because select_cpu did not insert p, the core calls enqueue. scx_simple inserts p into its shared DSQ, ordered by p's vtime, with a 20 ms slice.
CPU 2's current task stops. Its local DSQ and the global DSQ are empty, so the core calls dispatch for CPU 2.
dispatch moves the lowest-vtime task from DSQ 0 into CPU 2's local DSQ. Here that is p. The CPU it actually runs on is decided now, not at select_cpu time.
p starts. running() lets scx_simple advance its global vtime_now. The timer tick keeps charging p's slice.
When the slice hits zero (or p blocks), stopping() fires and scx_simple charges p's vtime by the time used, scaled by weight. Next lesson computes that charge.

blocks.prompt: Now suppose select_cpu finds CPU 5 idle and calls scx_bpf_dsq_insert(p, SCX_DSQ_LOCAL, ...). Which callbacks from the diagram above are skipped?
blocks.reveal: Both `ops.enqueue()` and `ops.dispatch()`. Inserting directly from `select_cpu` skips enqueue, and `SCX_DSQ_LOCAL` from select_cpu means the local DSQ of the CPU it returns (CPU 5), so CPU 5, which was just woken, finds p already in its local DSQ. This fast path is exactly what the kernel's default `select_cpu` does, and `scx_simple` counts it as its `local` statistic.

blocks.title: scx_simple's decision callbacks, traced for one wakeup

scenes.caption: p wakes with prev_cpu 2. The default idle-CPU search runs inside the kernel and reports no idle CPU.
Nothing was inserted, so 2 is returned as a hint and the core goes on to call enqueue.
enqueue reads p's vtime. p slept a long time, so its vtime is far behind the global vtime_now. Numbers in ms for readability.
The clamp limits sleeper credit to one slice: vtime becomes 10000 - 20 = 9980, then p is inserted into the shared DSQ.
Later a CPU finds its local and global DSQs empty. dispatch moves the head of the shared DSQ (lowest vtime) to that CPU.
When p starts running, vtime_now only moves forward: it is already 10000, so it stays 10000.
p used its whole slice (scx.slice is 0). With weight 100 (nice 0) the charge is 20 x 100/100 = 20, so p's vtime becomes 10000.

blocks.md: Where a task finally runs is decided when it lands in a local DSQ, usually inside `ops.dispatch()` on the CPU that is asking for work. `select_cpu` is an optimization: matching the final CPU saves a bit of work, and picking an idle CPU wakes it up.

Stashing a task in a BPF map from `select_cpu` does not skip `enqueue`; only a DSQ insertion does. The docs call storing tasks from `select_cpu` racy and discouraged. Also, the core ignores an invalid CPU choice such as one outside the task's allowed cpumask (the set of CPUs a task may run on, set with `sched_setaffinity()`).

blocks.question: Your scheduler's select_cpu always returns CPU 0 for every task but never inserts anything. Your enqueue puts every task in one shared custom DSQ, and dispatch moves from it. Where do tasks actually run?
options: On whichever CPU calls dispatch and moves them to its local DSQ, so across all CPUs
Only on CPU 0, because select_cpu pins the task there
On CPU 0 for the first slice, then anywhere
The core rejects the scheduler for returning the same CPU every time
blocks.explain: select_cpu's return value is a non-binding hint (and the CPU it wakes if idle). Without an insertion there, the task goes through enqueue into the shared DSQ, and any CPU running dispatch can move it to its own local DSQ.

blocks.question: A task is in your custom DSQ and your scheduler never implemented ops.dispatch(). The local and global DSQs on every CPU stay empty. What happens to the task?
options: The core consumes custom DSQs automatically after the global DSQ
It waits forever, so the watchdog eventually declares a stall and unloads the scheduler
The task is promoted to the global DSQ after one SCX_SLICE_DFL
The kernel calls the default dispatch, which drains all custom DSQs
blocks.explain: Only local and global DSQs are consumed automatically. Tasks in custom DSQs move only when ops.dispatch() (or another callback) moves them. A runnable task that never runs trips the watchdog, covered in lesson 9.

lessons.title: Worked example: weighted vtime fairness in a few lines of BPF

blocks.md:
`scx_simple` gets proportional fairness from one number per task, `p->scx.dsq_vtime`, and one rule: the shared DSQ is ordered by vtime, smallest first. A task that runs gets charged vtime; a task with a higher weight is charged less for the same CPU time, so it comes back to the front sooner.

Weights come from nice values. The fair class maps each nice value to a weight through its `sched_prio_to_weight` table: nice 0 is 1024, and each nice step multiplies or divides the weight by about 1.25 (nice 1 is 820). So two CPU-bound threads one nice level apart split a CPU about 55 to 45, since 1024 / (1024 + 820) is 55.5 percent. sched_ext hands BPF a different scale, the cgroup one, where the default weight is 100: the core multiplies the table weight by 100, divides by 1024 and rounds to the nearest integer, so nice 0 maps exactly to 100 and `p->scx.weight` lies in 1 to 10000.

blocks.caption: Left: the weight w that BPF sees is the nice-table weight times 100 over 1024, rounded (sched_weight_to_cgroup()). Right: the vtime charge is the slice time used, the default slice minus what is left, times 100 over w (scx_simple's stopping()).

blocks.md:
So a weight-100 task is charged its real run time, and a weight-305 task about a third of it. Computed from the kernel's `sched_prio_to_weight` table: nice 0 gives $1024 \to 100$, nice -5 gives $3121 \to 305$, nice 5 gives $335 \to 33$, nice -10 gives $9548 \to 932$.

Now the order of events, which decides the outcome. When a running task's slice ends, the core first calls `ops.dispatch(cpu, prev)`. Only after dispatch has moved the next task does it call `stopping()` on prev (the vtime charge) and `enqueue()` (back into the DSQ). `scx_simple`'s dispatch ignores `prev`, so **the task whose slice just ended never competes in that pick**.

Take the prerequisite course's machine: a build A and a test run B at nice 0 ($w = 100$) and a backup C at nice 5 ($w = 33$), all CPU-bound on one CPU, all starting at vtime 0. A full 20 ms slice costs A or B 20 ms of vtime and costs C $20 \times 100/33 = 60.606$ ms. Ties in the DSQ go to the task queued first.

blocks.title: Real scx_simple order on one CPU (v = vtime in ms at pick)

scenes.caption: All three start at vtime 0, so the DSQ serves them in arrival order: A, B, C. Each time a slice ends, dispatch takes the DSQ head before the finished task is charged and queued again.
C was charged 60.606 for its slice. A and B (20 per slice) alternate: whenever one finishes, the other has the lowest vtime among the tasks that are waiting.
At 180 ms B has just finished and the waiting tasks are A at 80 and C at 60.606, so C runs. Then the cycle repeats: six slices shared by A and B, one for C.
After 280 ms (14 slices) A ran 120 ms, B 120 ms and C 40 ms: 3/7, 3/7 and 1/7 per cycle, close to the weight ratio 100 : 100 : 33 (42.9, 42.9 and 14.2 percent).

blocks.prompt: Remove B. Now only A (nice 0, weight 100) and a task D at nice -5 (weight 305) share the CPU. Under real scx_simple, what share does D get?
blocks.reveal: **50 percent, not 75.3.** With two tasks the DSQ holds exactly one waiting task whenever a slice ends, and dispatch must take it, because the task that just ran is not back in the queue yet. So A and D strictly alternate whatever their weights. In general, on one CPU no task can run two slices in a row while another waits, so none gets more than half. Shares follow the weights only while no task's weight share is above one half.

blocks.code:
# One CPU, CPU-bound tasks, scx_simple vtime mode, in kernel order:
# dispatch moves the DSQ head, THEN prev is charged and re-enqueued.
SLICE = 20_000_000                       # SCX_SLICE_DFL, ns

def shares(weights, n=7000):
    v = dict.fromkeys(weights, 0)
    dsq = [(0, i, t) for i, t in enumerate(weights)]  # (vtime, seq, task)
    vnow, seq, runs = 0, len(weights), dict.fromkeys(weights, 0)
    dsq.sort(); cur = dsq.pop(0)[2]
    for _ in range(n):
        runs[cur] += 1
        prev = cur
        if dsq:                          # simple_dispatch: head of DSQ
            dsq.sort(); cur = dsq.pop(0)[2]
        v[prev] += SLICE * 100 // weights[prev]           # simple_stopping
        if cur != prev:                                   # simple_enqueue
            v[prev] = max(v[prev], vnow - SLICE)
            dsq.append((v[prev], seq, prev)); seq += 1
        vnow = max(vnow, v[cur])                          # simple_running
    return {t: round(100 * r / n, 1) for t, r in runs.items()}

print(shares({"A": 100, "B": 100, "C": 33}))  # nice 0, 0, 5
print(shares({"A": 100, "B": 305}))           # nice 0, -5
print(shares({"A": 100, "B": 100, "C": 305})) # nice 0, 0, -5
blocks.caption: Python 3 model of the callbacks above, run over 7000 slices. Output: {'A': 42.9, 'B': 42.9, 'C': 14.2}, then {'A': 50.0, 'B': 50.0}, then {'A': 25.0, 'B': 25.0, 'C': 50.0}.

blocks.title: Weight ratio versus real scx_simple: two nice 0 tasks and one nice -5

scenes.caption: The weight ratio 100 : 100 : 305 would give C 305/505 = 60.4 percent and A and B 19.8 each.
Real scx_simple (the model above): C is capped at 50 percent because it can never run two slices in a row, and A and B split the rest, 25 percent each.

blocks.md: Production schedulers close this gap in dispatch. `scx_bpfland`'s source describes the same trap: the kernel calls `ops.dispatch()` before it puts prev back, so taking the queue head "hands the CPU over in strict rotation, and a nice 19 task got as much of it as a nice 0 one". Its fix: charge prev for what it ran and, if prev still wins against the queue head, refill prev's slice with `scx_bpf_task_set_slice()` and return. When `ops.dispatch()` returns and prev is still runnable with slice left, the core keeps running prev.

blocks.caption: Sketch of a prev-aware dispatch for scx_simple, not run here (needs a sched_ext kernel). It charges prev itself because stopping() will not run for a slice that continues. In the Python model this rule gives 24.7/75.3 and 19.8/19.8/60.4: the weight ratios.

blocks.title: Weight-ratio share of task B against task A

scenes.caption: What weights promise: B's share is wB / (wA + wB). The fair class and a prev-aware dispatch deliver this; plain scx_simple on one CPU caps any task at 50 percent.
Raise A's weight to 305 (nice -5): B now needs weight 305 just to get half. Shares depend only on the weight ratio.

blocks.prompt: On a 4-CPU machine, task S slept for 10 s while vtime_now advanced from 0 to 10000 ms. Eight CPU-bound nice-0 tasks sit near vtime 10000. S wakes with dsq_vtime 0 and turns CPU-bound. Without the clamp in enqueue, what happens?
blocks.reveal: S has the lowest vtime at every pick it waits for, and keeps it for longer than it slept. It cannot run two slices in a row on one CPU (dispatch picks before S is queued again), but within a few ms another CPU's slice ends and picks it, so S runs about 80 percent of the time while the eight others share the remaining 3.2 CPUs. Their vtimes keep rising too, about 0.4 ms per ms each, so S gains only about 0.4 ms per ms on them: with evenly spaced slice ends, closing the 10000 ms gap takes about 25 s. That is the classic sleeper problem. scx_simple clamps S's vtime to `vtime_now - SCX_SLICE_DFL` = 9980, so S is at most one slice ahead.

blocks.title: Sleeper credit with and without scx_simple's clamp

scenes.caption: Unclamped: S wakes 10000 ms of vtime behind the CPU-bound tasks and wins almost every pick it waits for, for about 25 s: longer than it slept, since the others' vtimes keep rising while it catches up.
Clamped in enqueue to vtime_now - 20 ms: S is only 20 ms ahead, gets one slice of priority, then joins the rotation.

blocks.md: Weighted vtime in sched_ext takes a few lines: order a custom DSQ by vtime, charge `used x 100 / weight` in `stopping`, and cap how far behind a waking task's vtime may be. Whether the weights actually hold depends on whether prev competes in `dispatch`; `scx_simple`'s does not, so on one CPU no task gets more than half.

scx_simple charges `SCX_SLICE_DFL - p->scx.slice`. Its own comment warns that a task that yields has its slice zeroed and so is charged a full slice. Precise schedulers take explicit timestamps in `running` and `stopping` instead.

blocks.question: Under real scx_simple on one CPU, two CPU-bound tasks share it: one at nice 0 (weight 100) and one at nice 5 (weight 33). Roughly what share does the nice-5 task get in the long run?
options: About 25 percent, the weight ratio 33 / 133
About 33 percent
About 10 percent
About 50 percent: dispatch always takes the only waiting task, so the two alternate
blocks.explain: With two tasks, the task whose slice ended is not yet back in the DSQ when dispatch picks, so the other one always runs next. The weights change vtimes but never the order. With a prev-aware dispatch, or under the fair class, the nice-5 task would get about 25 percent.

blocks.question: You remove the clamp from scx_simple's enqueue. Which symptom appears first?
options: CPU-bound tasks starve each other in a round-robin cycle
A task waking from a long sleep wins nearly every pick for even longer than it slept, starving CPU-bound tasks
The verifier rejects the program because vtime can underflow
Nice values stop having any effect
blocks.explain: A sleeper's vtime stays where it was while running tasks keep advancing. Without the cap the waker is far behind and wins every pick it waits for until it catches up, which takes longer than the sleep because the others' vtimes keep rising: on a multi-CPU machine it runs almost continuously, hopping between CPUs, while the CPU-bound tasks share what is left.

lessons.title: Build, load and run your own scheduler end to end

blocks.md:
So far you have read callbacks. A working scheduler is two programs: the BPF side, compiled to BPF bytecode and loaded into the kernel, and a small user-space loader that loads and attaches it, prints statistics, and reports why it exited. In the kernel tree, `scx_simple` is 161 lines of BPF C and 110 lines of loader, and it is a complete scheduler.

First, the C conventions that the bpftrace prerequisite never showed. clang compiles a BPF C file into an object file whose ELF sections say what each piece is: `SEC("name")` puts a function or variable in a named section, maps are structs declared in the `.maps` section, and `_license` declares the license the kernel checks before allowing GPL-only kernel functions. **libbpf** (the loading library) and **bpftool** (the kernel's BPF command-line tool) read those sections.

The BPF side has four parts beyond the callbacks you know:

- **`BPF_STRUCT_OPS(name, args...)`** expands to `SEC("struct_ops/name")` plus `BPF_PROG` (a libbpf macro that gives the function typed arguments), marking a function as a struct_ops callback. `BPF_STRUCT_OPS_SLEEPABLE` marks one that may sleep, such as `init`.
- **`SCX_OPS_DEFINE(simple_ops, ...)`** declares the `struct sched_ext_ops` in the `.struct_ops.link` section, so it can be attached as a link.
- **A per-CPU array map** `stats` holds two counters (direct local insertions and shared-queue insertions).
- **`UEI_DEFINE(uei)`** declares user exit info, a global that `UEI_RECORD()` fills in `ops.exit()` with the exit kind, reason and message.

blocks.caption: The BPF half of scx_simple, abridged from tools/sched_ext/scx_simple.bpf.c (the real init also reports a failure with scx_bpf_error; the real table lists all eight callbacks).

blocks.md: The loader uses the generated *skeleton*, a header that bpftool writes from the BPF object with typed pointers to its maps, programs and globals (build step 3 below). `SCX_OPS_OPEN` opens it; command-line options then set read-only globals (`skel->rodata->fifo_sched = true`), which must happen before load because `const volatile` globals become constants the verifier can reason about. `SCX_OPS_LOAD` loads and verifies, `SCX_OPS_ATTACH` calls `bpf_map__attach_struct_ops` and returns the link. Then it polls once a second until Ctrl-C or until `UEI_EXITED` says the kernel ended the scheduler, destroys the link, and `UEI_REPORT` prints the reason. If the exit code asks for a restart (for example after CPU hotplug), it starts over.

blocks.caption: The user-space loader, abridged from tools/sched_ext/scx_simple.c. The SCX_OPS_* and UEI_* macros come from tools/sched_ext/include/scx.

blocks.title: Life of a scheduler process, from load to exit report

scenes.caption: SCX_OPS_LOAD loads every program and map. The verifier must accept all of them before anything is attached.
SCX_OPS_ATTACH creates the struct_ops link. The core calls ops.init(), which creates DSQ 0, and then switches tasks to the ext class.
Every second the loader reads the per-CPU stats map: one value per possible CPU, which it sums.
If something goes wrong (scx_bpf_error, an invalid argument, the watchdog), the core calls ops.exit(), where UEI_RECORD copies the reason into a global the loader can read.
The loop ends, the loader destroys the link and UEI_REPORT prints the debug dump and the EXIT line. Every task is already back on the fair class.

blocks.md:
Building follows `tools/sched_ext/Makefile` and its README. You need clang 16 or newer (the BPF programs must be compiled with clang), pahole 1.25 or newer (the tool that turns the kernel's debug info into BTF), and a kernel built with `CONFIG_SCHED_CLASS_EXT=y` plus the BPF and BTF options listed in lesson 9. The Makefile then:

1. writes `vmlinux.h`, every kernel type as C, with `bpftool btf dump file <vmlinux> format c`, reading BTF from the first vmlinux it finds: the kernel tree's own build (as in the VM flow below), else the running kernel's `/sys/kernel/btf/vmlinux`,
2. compiles each `.bpf.c` with `clang -target bpf -g -O2`,
3. runs `bpftool gen skeleton` on the object to produce `scx_simple.bpf.skel.h`, a header with typed pointers to its maps, programs and globals,
4. compiles the loader against libbpf.

Run it inside a virtual machine: a broken scheduler can starve threads for tens of seconds, and loading one needs root.

blocks.md: **Exercise 1: a per-task counter.** BPF task storage (`BPF_MAP_TYPE_TASK_STORAGE`) is a map whose values hang off each `task_struct`, so a scheduler can keep private per-task state. The kernel's `scx_userland` uses it exactly this way: create the entry in `ops.init_task()` with `BPF_LOCAL_STORAGE_GET_F_CREATE`, look it up without that flag elsewhere. Add `.init_task`, `.exit_task` and the new `running` code to `scx_simple`, rebuild, and read the output with `cat /sys/kernel/tracing/trace_pipe`.

blocks.caption: Exercise 1 code, modeled on scx_userland's task_ctx_stor. Not run here.

blocks.prompt: **Exercise 2: break it on purpose.** Empty the body of `simple_dispatch()` and rerun. Which tasks still run, what does the loader print, and roughly when?
blocks.reveal: Tasks that `select_cpu` finds an idle CPU for still run (they go straight to a local DSQ), and a CPU whose dispatch finds nothing keeps running its previous task. Everything enqueued into DSQ 0 waits forever. With the default 30 s timeout the watchdog fires 30 to 45 s later (lesson 9), and the loader prints a debug dump and a line built from these strings in `ext.c`: `EXIT: runnable task stall (<comm>[<pid>] failed to run for <s>.<ms>s) on CPU <n>`. Set `.timeout_ms = 5000` in `SCX_OPS_DEFINE` to see it within 5 to 7.5 s.

blocks.md: A scheduler is two programs: a BPF object (callbacks plus maps, gathered in one `sched_ext_ops` struct_ops map) and a loader that opens it, sets read-only options, loads, attaches, polls and reports why it exited. Exiting the loader is the unload.

Misconception: the loader is just a launcher and can exit once the scheduler is attached. The link belongs to the process: when it exits, the link is destroyed and the kernel unregisters the scheduler. The loader is also the only place the exit reason gets printed.

blocks.question: Your loader opened and loaded the skeleton without errors, but /sys/kernel/sched_ext/state still says disabled. Which step is missing?
options: The verifier has not run yet
Creating DSQ 0
Attaching the struct_ops map (SCX_OPS_ATTACH, bpf_map__attach_struct_ops)
Setting a nice value on the loader
blocks.explain: Loading only verifies and loads programs and maps. The scheduler becomes active when the struct_ops map is attached as a link; ops.init(), which creates DSQ 0, runs as part of that registration.

blocks.question: scx_simple's stats map is a BPF_MAP_TYPE_PERCPU_ARRAY and stat_inc() does a plain (*cnt_p)++. Why is that safe without atomics?
options: Each CPU increments its own copy of the counter, and the loader sums the copies
BPF programs never run on two CPUs at the same time
The verifier inserts a lock around every map update
It is not safe; the counts are only approximate
blocks.explain: A per-CPU array keeps one value per possible CPU, and a BPF program updates the copy of the CPU it runs on. bpf_map_lookup_elem from user space returns all copies, which read_stats() adds up.

lessons.title: Placement and preemption: idle CPUs, kicks, LOCAL_ON and locality

blocks.md: `scx_simple` has one queue and never preempts. Real machines need more. Picture 8 CPUs in two groups of 4, each group sharing one L3 cache, the *last-level cache* (LLC). Task p last ran on CPU 1 and wakes while CPU 2 (same L3) and CPU 6 (other L3) are idle: which should it get? And if no CPU is idle and p is urgent, how do you take a CPU away from a running task? This lesson covers the four tools: built-in idle tracking, kicking a CPU, inserting with `LOCAL_ON`, and queues per cache.

sched_ext keeps a built-in **idle cpumask**, a bitmap with one bit per CPU that is set while the CPU is idle. `scx_bpf_select_cpu_dfl(p, prev_cpu, wake_flags, &is_idle)` is the default policy over it, the one `scx_simple` calls. Its order, from `kernel/sched/ext/idle.c`:

1. a CPU on a fully idle core (SMT, simultaneous multithreading, puts two hardware threads on one core; a fully idle core has both idle),
2. `prev_cpu`, for warm L1 and L2 caches,
3. an idle SMT sibling of `prev_cpu`,
4. an idle CPU in the same LLC,
5. one in the same NUMA node (on machines where memory is split per socket, the CPUs attached to the same memory bank),
6. any idle CPU the task is allowed on.

Steps 4 and 5 run only when the machine has several LLCs or nodes.

blocks.title: Default idle CPU selection on 2 LLCs x 4 CPUs

scenes.caption: Task p last ran on CPU 1 and wakes. CPU 1 is busy, so step 2 (reuse prev_cpu) fails. Assume no SMT siblings, so steps 1 and 3 do not apply.
Step 4: an idle CPU in prev_cpu's LLC. CPU 2 shares CPU 1's L3, where p's data may still be warm. scx_bpf_select_cpu_dfl() returns 2 with is_idle = true.
If CPU 2 were busy too, step 5 is skipped (one NUMA node here) and step 6 takes any allowed idle CPU: CPU 6, in the other LLC. p runs at once but with a cold L3.
With no idle CPU at all, the helper returns prev_cpu with is_idle = false. Nothing is inserted, so the core goes on to ops.enqueue().

blocks.md: To choose yourself, `scx_bpf_pick_idle_cpu(cpus_allowed, flags)` finds an idle CPU and *claims* it: it clears that CPU's idle bit, so a second waker cannot pick the same one. `SCX_PICK_IDLE_CORE` asks for a whole idle core. It returns `-EBUSY` when nothing is idle, and the kernel's own comment warns that this result can race with CPUs that are just going idle. A scheduler that concludes "all busy, so someone will dispatch soon" can stall with idle CPUs and queued tasks; to guarantee a dispatch, use `scx_bpf_pick_any_cpu()` and kick that CPU.

**Kicking** makes another CPU run its scheduling path: `scx_bpf_kick_cpu(cpu, flags)`.

- `SCX_KICK_IDLE`: wake the CPU only if it is idle; it then goes through at least one full scheduling cycle (so it calls `ops.dispatch()`) before idling again.
- `SCX_KICK_PREEMPT`: preempt the current task. Its slice is set to zero, so it expires and the CPU runs the dispatch path.
- `SCX_KICK_WAIT`: return only after the target CPU's current task has switched out.

Inserting into a local DSQ with `SCX_ENQ_PREEMPT` does preemption in one step: the task goes to the head of that local DSQ, the running task's slice is zeroed and the CPU is kicked. `SCX_DSQ_LOCAL_ON | cpu` (lesson 3's id layout) names any CPU's local DSQ, from any callback.

blocks.caption: Sketch, not run here. is_urgent() stands for whatever signal your scheduler uses. LOCAL_ON to a CPU outside the task's allowed cpumask is an error that unloads the scheduler, so a real version checks p->cpus_ptr first, as scx_central does.

blocks.md: What happens to `prev` when a CPU's dispatch finds nothing? By default the core keeps running it with a fresh `SCX_SLICE_DFL` slice and counts `SCX_EV_DISPATCH_KEEP_LAST`. With the `SCX_OPS_ENQ_LAST` flag, prev is instead passed to `ops.enqueue()` with `SCX_ENQ_LAST`: if the scheduler puts it back in this CPU's local DSQ it keeps running, otherwise the CPU goes idle. Schedulers that keep tasks elsewhere use this to see every decision.

**Locality.** One shared queue balances perfectly, but every CPU contends on it and tasks hop between caches freely; `scx_simple`'s header says it suits a single uniform L3. The alternative is a queue per LLC. In `scx_rusty`, the BPF side keeps one domain per LLC by default and orders each domain's queue by a weighted virtual deadline (plain FIFO with `--fifo-sched`). Its dispatch first moves a task from its own domain's DSQ; if that is empty, it *steals* from another domain on the same NUMA node ("greedy" stealing, on by default; stolen tasks keep their home domain). A Rust user-space balancer runs every 2 s by default, computes each domain's load, and tells BPF which tasks to move for good.

blocks.title: Per-LLC queues with stealing, scx_rusty style

scenes.caption: Uneven load: six tasks wait in LLC 0's queue, none in LLC 1's. CPUs 6 and 7 (LLC 1) just went idle. Queue lengths 6 and 0.
CPU 6 runs dispatch: its own LLC's queue is empty, so it steals from another domain on the same NUMA node. T1 moves to CPU 6. Queues 5 and 0.
CPU 7 steals T2: queues 4 and 0. The cost: T1 and T2 last ran under LLC 0, so their data sits in that L3 and their first accesses on CPUs 6 and 7 miss.
Simplified: about every 2 s the user-space balancer compares domain loads and assigns some tasks a new home domain (target_dom); from then on they queue in LLC 1. Queues 2 and 2.

blocks.md: At the far end sits `scx_central`: one CPU makes every decision. Other CPUs' dispatch only raises a "gimme" flag and kicks the central CPU with `SCX_KICK_PREEMPT`. The central CPU's dispatch pops task ids from a BPF queue map, inserts each with `SCX_DSQ_LOCAL_ON | cpu`, and kicks that CPU with `SCX_KICK_IDLE`. Tasks get `SCX_SLICE_INF`, an infinite slice, so on `CONFIG_NO_HZ_FULL` kernels booted with `nohz_full` the worker CPUs can stop their timer tick; a 1 ms BPF timer preempts CPUs whose task has used its slice. The use case the kernel README gives: VMs, where running with infinite slices and no timer tick avoids unnecessary, expensive vmexits (switches from the guest back to the host).
Placement is decided when a task lands in a local DSQ. `select_cpu` and the idle cpumask choose where, `LOCAL_ON` puts it there from any CPU, and kicks (`IDLE`, `PREEMPT`) decide when that CPU looks.

Misconception: if no idle CPU was found, a busy CPU will pick the task up soon. Only CPUs that run their dispatch path do, and idle tracking races with CPUs going idle. Inserting into a queue no CPU will look at, with no kick, is how schedulers stall while CPUs idle.

blocks.question: Your enqueue inserts a task into custom DSQ 3 while CPU 5 is idle. Nothing kicks CPU 5, and the other CPUs never read DSQ 3 in their dispatch. What can happen?
options: CPU 5 polls custom DSQs and notices within one tick
The kernel moves custom DSQ tasks to the global DSQ after one slice
The task waits while CPU 5 stays idle, until some CPU happens to dispatch from DSQ 3 or the watchdog fires
The verifier rejects enqueue callbacks that do not kick a CPU
blocks.explain: An idle CPU runs the scheduling path only when it is woken: by select_cpu choosing it, by a kick, or by new work in its local DSQ. Custom DSQs are only read by dispatch callbacks, so an unread queue plus no kick leaves the task stranded.

blocks.question: A latency-critical thread wakes while every CPU runs batch tasks with 20 ms slices. Which choice gets it running within microseconds instead of after up to 20 ms?
options: Give it a vtime lower than everyone's in the shared DSQ
Insert it into its CPU's local DSQ with SCX_ENQ_PREEMPT
Call scx_bpf_kick_cpu(cpu, SCX_KICK_IDLE) on its last CPU
Return its last CPU from select_cpu
blocks.explain: SCX_ENQ_PREEMPT zeroes the running task's slice and kicks the CPU, and the woken task is at the head of that local DSQ. A low vtime only puts it first in line for the next slice end; KICK_IDLE does nothing to a busy CPU; select_cpu's return value is a hint.

blocks.question: Why does scx_rusty's dispatch try its own domain's DSQ before stealing from another LLC's?
options: The kernel forbids moving a task between LLCs
Stealing is reserved for the user-space balancer
Domain DSQs are FIFO while others are vtime ordered
Its own domain's tasks most likely still have data in this L3, so they start warm
blocks.explain: Every CPU in a domain shares one L3. A task queued there probably ran there recently. Stealing balances load at the price of a cold cache, so rusty does it only when its own queue is empty.

lessons.title: Keeping tasks in BPF: custody, dequeue and user-space policy

blocks.md: `scx_simple` hands every task straight to a DSQ. Many schedulers instead hold tasks in their own structures: one BPF list per priority, a tree, even a queue that a user-space process reads. Then the kernel must tell the scheduler when a task it holds has to leave. A tiny case: task T waits in your nice-0 list and an administrator runs `renice -n -10` on it. If your scheduler never hears about it, T stays in the wrong list, or your list keeps an entry for a task the kernel has already taken back.

The kernel docs call this **custody**: the BPF scheduler is responsible for the task. A task enters custody when `ops.enqueue()` inserts it into a custom DSQ or stores it in BPF data structures. Inserting it into a *terminal* DSQ (`SCX_DSQ_LOCAL`, `SCX_DSQ_LOCAL_ON | cpu` or `SCX_DSQ_GLOBAL`) means no custody, and no `ops.dequeue()` later.

When a task leaves custody, `ops.dequeue(p, deq_flags)` is called exactly once. The flags say why: none for a regular dispatch to a terminal DSQ, `SCX_DEQ_CORE_SCHED_EXEC` when core scheduling (the `CONFIG_SCHED_CORE` feature that only lets mutually trusted tasks share an SMT core) picks it, and `SCX_DEQ_SCHED_CHANGE` when a property (affinity, policy, nice, a CPU migration) changes while it waits. For a custom DSQ the kernel removes the task itself and `dequeue` is a notification; for a task in your own BPF structure, removing it there is your job.

blocks.title: One task's life under a sched_ext scheduler (kernel docs pseudo-code)

scenes.caption: A new task: init_task() lets the scheduler set up per-task state (and may refuse it), enable() marks the start of BPF scheduling for it.
The task wakes: select_cpu() if it can migrate, then runnable(), then enqueue(). Suppose enqueue puts it in a custom DSQ or a BPF list: it is now in the scheduler's custody.
While it waits, someone changes its nice value. It leaves custody through dequeue() with SCX_DEQ_SCHED_CHANGE, then quiescent(), set_weight(), runnable(), and the loop enqueues it again.
A CPU's dispatch() moves it to a local DSQ, which also ends custody: dequeue() with no special flag. Exactly one dequeue per stay in custody.
It runs: running(), a tick() every 1/HZ, and at slice end dispatch() on that CPU, which may refill the slice to keep it running (lesson 5's fix).
stopping() when it leaves the CPU. If it blocked, quiescent() too; if it was still runnable, the loop enqueues it again.
When it leaves SCHED_EXT or exits: disable(), then exit_task() to free per-task state.

blocks.md: `scx_qmap`, the kernel's multi-level FIFO example, keeps queued tasks in five FIFOs: arena-backed doubly linked lists. A BPF *arena* is a memory region shared by BPF programs and user space, and each list is threaded through a link stored in every task's context. `weight_to_idx()` maps weight to a FIFO (at most 25, at most 50, below 200, below 400, the rest), and each CPU's dispatch round-robins them, taking up to $2^i$ tasks from FIFO $i$ so heavier FIFOs get more turns. `qmap_dequeue()` unlinks the task from whichever FIFO holds it.

blocks.title: scx_qmap's five FIFOs when a queued task is reniced

scenes.caption: Task T (nice 0, weight 100) waits in FIFO 2 with two other nice-0 tasks. One task of each other FIFO: nice 10 (11), nice 5 (33), nice -5 (305), nice -10 (932).
renice -n -10 on T. The kernel calls qmap_dequeue(T, SCX_DEQ_SCHED_CHANGE), which unlinks T from FIFO 2. Then set_weight(T, 932) and runnable(T).
The kernel calls qmap_enqueue(T) again; weight_to_idx(932) is 4, so T joins FIFO 4. Each CPU's dispatch round-robins the FIFOs, taking up to 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 tasks from FIFO 0 to 4.
Without a dequeue callback, T's one list link (kept in its task context) would still be threaded into FIFO 2 when enqueue links it into FIFO 4: a corrupted list, or a stale entry dispatched later.

blocks.prompt: A task waits in scx_qmap's FIFO 2. An administrator pins it to one CPU with taskset. Which callbacks run, in order, before it is queued again?
blocks.reveal: `ops.dequeue()` with `SCX_DEQ_SCHED_CHANGE` (qmap unlinks it from FIFO 2), `ops.quiescent()`, the property change callback, here `ops.set_cpumask()` for the new affinity, then `ops.runnable()` and `ops.enqueue()`. Its weight did not change, so it goes back into FIFO 2, now as a task with only one allowed CPU.

blocks.md: Custody also covers the most extreme design: a policy in user space. In the kernel's `scx_userland`, tasks pinned to fewer than all CPUs stay in the kernel in FIFO order. For the rest, `enqueue` pushes the pid, runtime and weight into a `BPF_MAP_TYPE_QUEUE` map; a single-threaded user-space scheduler drains it, keeps a vruntime-sorted list, and writes chosen pids into a second queue map that `dispatch` drains into the global DSQ. Its own header notes that ring buffer maps (`BPF_MAP_TYPE_RINGBUF`, `BPF_MAP_TYPE_USER_RINGBUF`) would exchange messages more efficiently.

blocks.title: scx_userland: a decision that goes through user space

scenes.caption: Task p wakes and may run on any CPU. userland_enqueue() pushes its pid, runtime and weight into the enqueued queue map and sets a flag that user space needs to run.
A CPU calls dispatch. Nothing is decided yet, so all it can do is insert the user-space scheduler's own thread into the global DSQ so that it gets a CPU.
The user-space thread runs: it drains the enqueued map, orders tasks by vruntime in a sorted list, and pushes the chosen pids into the dispatched map.
Only on a later dispatch does p reach the global DSQ and a CPU. Every decision waited for a user-space thread to be scheduled and run.

blocks.md: The cost is the round trip: no task can be placed until the user-space thread has itself been scheduled, has run, and has written back. The scx project drew that conclusion in November 2026 when it [removed scx_rustland and its framework](https://github.com/sched-ext/scx/commit/0e63ecb1a12a84b6d2ff94d848ffca82e4555cbb) in favor of scx_rustsched, which runs Rust scheduling policy in BPF "avoiding rustland's scheduling round trips to user space". User space still does slower work well, as scx_rusty's load balancer shows.

If you hold a task anywhere other than a terminal DSQ, implement `ops.dequeue()` and drop your reference there. The kernel will re-enqueue the task after any property change, so a stale entry means a task is queued twice.
Misconception: once a task is in a custom DSQ it is on its way to a CPU. It is in your custody until dispatch moves it, and a property change can pull it back out through `ops.dequeue()` at any time.

blocks.question: ops.enqueue() inserts task T directly into SCX_DSQ_GLOBAL. Before T runs, its nice value changes. Is ops.dequeue() called for T?
options: Yes, with SCX_DEQ_SCHED_CHANGE
No: the global DSQ is terminal, so T never entered custody
Yes, with no flags
Only if the scheduler implements ops.set_weight()
blocks.explain: Custody starts only with a custom DSQ or BPF-side storage. Tasks sent to SCX_DSQ_LOCAL, LOCAL_ON or SCX_DSQ_GLOBAL are no longer the scheduler's business, so property changes do not produce ops.dequeue().

blocks.question: Your scheduler keeps waiting tasks in a BPF red-black tree and has no ops.dequeue(). A waiting task's CPU affinity changes. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing: the kernel removes the task from BPF data structures itself
The verifier rejects any scheduler that stores tasks without a dequeue callback
The task keeps its old affinity until it next sleeps
The kernel enqueues it again while the old node is still in the tree, so it can be found twice and dispatched from a stale entry
blocks.explain: The kernel does not know your tree. After the change it calls ops.enqueue() again, so without a dequeue that removed the old node the task now has two entries. The kernel ignores stale dispatches it can detect, but your data structure is already inconsistent.

lessons.title: Safety net, failure modes and schedulers in production

blocks.md:
The BPF verifier (prerequisite course) already guarantees at load time that callbacks terminate and only touch memory safely. But a perfectly memory-safe scheduler can still have a bad *policy*: it can forget a task in a custom DSQ forever. sched_ext adds runtime checks on top of the verifier:

- **Callback validation**: invalid return values or arguments (for example a bad DSQ id or enqueue flags) are errors that unload the scheduler.
- **`scx_bpf_error()`**: the scheduler can abort itself with a message.
- **Watchdog**: if any runnable task waits longer than `ops.timeout_ms` without running, the scheduler exits with `SCX_EXIT_ERROR_STALL`. The default and the maximum is 30 s.
- **SysRq-S**: an operator key sequence that forces the unload; SysRq-D dumps debug state without unloading.

blocks.title: Every failure path ends with tasks back on the fair class

nodes.label:
exit info + dump
to user space

scenes.caption: At load time the verifier proves memory safety and termination. A rejected program never becomes the scheduler, so nothing changes.
At run time, an invalid result (say, a bad DSQ id) or an explicit scx_bpf_error() triggers an error exit.
The watchdog catches policy bugs the verifier cannot: a task that is runnable but never picked. It reports the task name and how long it waited.
Operator or owner exits take the same road. During load, unload and error recovery the kernel runs in bypass mode with simple queues and 5 ms slices so every task makes progress.

blocks.md: How fast is a stall caught? All schedulers share one watchdog that runs every half of the timeout, and checks each CPU's runnable tasks against `runnable_at + timeout`. A task that stops being picked at time 0 becomes overdue at the timeout $T$, but the next check can come up to $T/2$ later. Ignoring jiffy rounding (the watchdog timer counts in whole ticks of 1/HZ), detection lands between $T$ and $1.5T$. The tick also checks that the watchdog itself has run within $T$.

blocks.title: Stall detection window versus ops.timeout_ms

scenes.caption: With the default 30 s timeout, a starved task is reported between 30 and 45 s after it stopped being scheduled. Simplified model: ignores jiffy granularity.
A scheduler can set a shorter timeout_ms (never above 30 s) to fail fast in testing: 5 s gives detection within 5 to 7.5 s.

blocks.md: Ignoring kernel bugs, the kernel's tools/sched_ext README puts the worst case plainly: a broken sched_ext scheduler can starve some threads until the watchdog fires. It cannot corrupt memory, and the machine returns to the fair scheduler on its own.

Running one in production involves a few more realities:

- **Kernel config**: `CONFIG_SCHED_CLASS_EXT`, `CONFIG_BPF_SYSCALL`, `CONFIG_BPF_JIT` and `CONFIG_DEBUG_INFO_BTF` (BTF, the BPF Type Format, is the kernel's description of its own types, which struct_ops needs to match `sched_ext_ops`), among others listed in the docs.
- **No ABI stability**: callbacks, constants and `scx_bpf_*` kfuncs (kernel functions that the kernel explicitly exports for BPF programs to call) may change between kernel versions, so schedulers track kernels (the dispatch helper renames after 6.12 are an example).
- **Knobs are the scheduler's job**: nice is delivered through `ops.set_weight()` and cgroup `cpu.weight` (a relative share, default 100), `cpu.max` (a hard cap: so much run time per period) and `cpu.idle` (marks the group as lowest priority) through cgroup callbacks. A scheduler may ignore them.
- **Observability**: `/sys/kernel/sched_ext/state`, `root/ops`, and the `root/events` counters (fallback CPU picks, default slice refills, bypass activations).

The [sched-ext/scx](https://github.com/sched-ext/scx) repository collects schedulers, mostly with Rust user-space parts. With lesson 2's EEVDF and lesson 7's placement tools in mind:

- **scx_rusty**: one domain per LLC with weighted vtime ordering in BPF, greedy stealing between domains, and a Rust user-space load balancer moving tasks between domains.
- **scx_lavd**: latency-criticality aware virtual deadline. It measures how latency-critical a task is and uses that for its deadline and time slice, with domains per LLC, core type (performance or efficiency cores) and NUMA node; motivated by gaming.
- **scx_bpfland**: EEVDF-like, with one deadline-ordered queue per CPU and all decisions in BPF; it sizes each task's request from how long it runs between sleeps.
- **scx_layered**: classifies tasks into configurable layers (for example by cgroup) with per-layer CPU guarantees.

Policy in user space is fading: scx_rustland was removed in November 2026 (lesson 8). Kernels can now also nest schedulers (`CONFIG_EXT_SUB_SCHED`): a parent delegates CPUs to child schedulers on cgroups.

Misconception: switching to a sched_ext scheduler is a free speedup. Each one encodes tradeoffs for a workload. scx_simple's own header says it suits a single uniform L3 and that its FIFO mode lets saturating threads drown out interactive ones. Benchmark your workload against the fair class (lesson 10 shows how), and check whether the scheduler honors the cgroup limits you rely on.

blocks.question: After switching a host to a sched_ext scheduler, a batch container's cpu.max limit is no longer enforced. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The verifier strips cgroup checks from BPF programs
cpu.max only applies to realtime tasks, which sched_ext does not handle
The kernel crashed back to bypass mode, where cgroups are ignored
cgroup CPU controls are passed to the BPF scheduler through callbacks and this scheduler does not implement them
blocks.explain: The kernel docs state the core reports cpu.max, cpu.weight and cpu.idle to the BPF scheduler via ops.cgroup_init() and cgroup_set_* callbacks, and each scheduler decides whether to implement them. Many ignore some of them, so read the scheduler's docs.

blocks.question: A scheduler with the default timeout has a bug: tasks of one cgroup are inserted into a custom DSQ that dispatch never reads. What do you observe?
options: Those tasks freeze, then within about 30 to 45 s the scheduler is unloaded with a stall error and everything runs on fair again
The machine hangs until rebooted because BPF code runs with interrupts disabled
The verifier refuses to load the scheduler because a DSQ is never consumed
The tasks run anyway because custom DSQs fall back to the global DSQ after one slice
blocks.explain: The verifier checks memory safety and termination, not whether your policy eventually runs every task. The watchdog sees runnable tasks older than 30 s on its next check (every 15 s), exits with SCX_EXIT_ERROR_STALL, and tasks revert to the fair class.

blocks.question: You are prototyping a new policy and want stalls reported in seconds, not tens of seconds. What do you change?
options: Raise SCX_SLICE_DFL so tasks run longer
Set ops.timeout_ms to a smaller value, such as 5000
Set ops.timeout_ms to 60000 so the watchdog runs more often
Enable SCX_OPS_SWITCH_PARTIAL
blocks.explain: timeout_ms sets the watchdog deadline and the check interval is half of it, so 5000 ms means detection within about 5 to 7.5 s. Values above 30000 are rejected, and slice length does not affect stall detection.

blocks.md: You loaded a scheduler and the game feels smoother. Is it? A scheduler changes three things you can measure: how long a woken task waits before it runs (*wakeup latency*), how much work finishes per second (*throughput*), and how CPU is split among competitors (*fairness*). Averages hide the problem. Take 100 wakeups: 98 wait 0.05 ms and 2 wait 30 ms. The mean is 0.649 ms and the median 0.05 ms, yet the *p99*, the value that 99 percent of samples are at or below, is 30 ms: a visible stutter.

Three tools cover most of it:

- **schbench**, by Chris Mason, reproduces a web workload: message threads post requests to worker threads, which do two short sleeps and some matrix math. It reports *wakeup latency* (from posting work to the worker running), *request latency* and requests per second, each as percentiles. It aims to saturate every CPU, and it makes preemption costly with a per-CPU lock held during the math.
- **perf sched**: `perf sched record` captures scheduling events and `perf sched latency` prints per task the runtime, the count, and the average and maximum *delay*, the time it was ready to run but kept waiting.
- **sched_ext's own**: the `root/events` counters, the `sched_ext_dump` tracepoint, SysRq-D, and the `scx_show_state.py` script.

blocks.code:
$ ./schbench -F 256 -n 5 --calibrate -r 10
setting worker threads to 52
...
Wakeup Latencies percentiles (usec) runtime 10 (s) (30212 total samples)
          50.0th: 7          (7806 samples)
          90.0th: 18         (8649 samples)
        * 99.0th: 175        (2590 samples)
          99.9th: 909        (271 samples)
          min=1, max=10224

blocks.md:
A fair comparison controls everything except the scheduler:

1. **Same kernel, same machine.** The baseline is the fair class (EEVDF) with no BPF scheduler loaded; the candidate is the same command after loading it.
2. **Warm up** and discard that period (`-w`).
3. **Repeat and alternate** A and B several times, so drift (temperature, background jobs) hits both.
4. **Report percentiles with spread**: p50 and p99 per run, and the range across runs, not one number.
5. **Sweep the load** below, at and above the CPU count; schedulers differ most at saturation.
6. **Watch throughput too**, since latency can be bought with lost requests per second.

blocks.code:
#!/bin/sh
# A/B on one kernel: fair class vs scx_simple, alternating, 5 runs each
for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do
  schbench -m 2 -t 16 -r 30 -w 5 -j fair-$i.json -J fair
  scx_simple > /dev/null &               # as root
  sleep 2; cat /sys/kernel/sched_ext/state   # expect: enabled
  schbench -m 2 -t 16 -r 30 -w 5 -j simple-$i.json -J simple
  kill %1; wait; sleep 2                 # back on the fair class
done
blocks.caption: Not run here. -m message threads, -t workers per message thread, -r runtime in s, -w warmup in s (stats reset after it), -j JSON output, -J job name. Repeat with -t below, at and above the CPU count.

blocks.md: What should you expect at saturation from `scx_simple`? A model shows the shape before you measure. Four CPUs, eight CPU-bound threads and four interactive threads that run 0.2 to 0.8 ms and sleep 5 to 15 ms; 20 ms slices, no preemption, the kernel's dispatch-then-enqueue order, one minute of simulated time (about 6,000 and 12,000 wakeups). In this model the four CPUs' slice ends drift into step, so waits cluster near multiples of 10 ms; a real machine will spread them out. With up to 5 ms of random jitter added to each slice in the same model, the vtime median drops to about 4.5 ms while the p99 stays near 15 ms: trust the tail more than the median here, and measure.

blocks.title: Simulated wakeup latency of interactive threads at saturation

scenes.caption: scx_simple -f (FIFO): a waking interactive thread queues behind every waiting CPU-bound thread. Median 30.1 ms, p99 34.9 ms, for work that needs under 1 ms. Simulated, not measured.
Default vtime mode: the sleeper sorts near the front but still waits for a slice to end somewhere, since scx_simple never preempts. Median 10.1 ms, p99 14.8 ms. Same model, same seed.

blocks.md: This is the warning in `scx_simple`'s own header: FIFO scheduling lets saturating threads drown out interactive ones. Vtime mode helps because a sleeper's vtime is low, but with no preemption it still waits for some slice to end. Under EEVDF a woken task with an earlier deadline can preempt the running one (lesson 2), so the real comparison with the fair class is the A/B measurement above, not this model.

When numbers look wrong, look inside. `root/events` counts what the core corrected for you: `SCX_EV_SELECT_CPU_FALLBACK` (select_cpu returned a CPU the task cannot use), `SCX_EV_DISPATCH_KEEP_LAST` (prev kept running because nothing else was queued), `SCX_EV_REFILL_SLICE_DFL` (a slice refilled with the 20 ms default) and the `SCX_EV_BYPASS_*` counters (time and dispatches in bypass mode). SysRq-D writes a debug dump of scheduler and task state to the `sched_ext_dump` tracepoint without unloading anything; on an error exit the loader prints the same kind of dump itself.

blocks.code:
cat /sys/kernel/sched_ext/state /sys/kernel/sched_ext/root/ops
cat /sys/kernel/sched_ext/root/events      # counters, one "name value" per line
tools/sched_ext/scx_show_state.py          # drgn (live kernel debugger) script: enable state, bypass depth

perf sched record -- sleep 10              # all CPUs, while the workload runs
perf sched latency --sort max              # per task: runtime, avg and max delay

cd /sys/kernel/tracing
echo 1 > events/sched_ext/sched_ext_dump/enable
echo D > /proc/sysrq-trigger               # SysRq-D: dump, scheduler keeps running
cat trace_pipe
blocks.caption: Not run here; run as root inside the test VM. Capital D: the sched_ext dump is registered on SysRq-D, while lowercase d is a different SysRq action.

blocks.md: Last, check the knobs you rely on (lesson 9: cgroup limits are the scheduler's job). Put a CPU-bound loop in a cgroup with `cpu.max` = `50000 100000`, 50 ms of CPU per 100 ms period, and read `usage_usec` from its `cpu.stat` 10 s apart. Enforced: about 5,000,000 us, 50 percent of a CPU. Ignored: about 10,000,000 us. `scx_flatcg` is a good test subject: its ops table implements `cgroup_set_weight` (hierarchical `cpu.weight`, flattened into one level) but no `cgroup_set_bandwidth`, the callback that receives `cpu.max`, so expect this test to show the cap ignored while a 2:1 `cpu.weight` test shows its weights honored.

blocks.code:
cd /sys/fs/cgroup
mkdir capped
echo +cpu > cgroup.subtree_control
echo "50000 100000" > capped/cpu.max       # 50 ms per 100 ms: half a CPU
sh -c 'echo $$ > capped/cgroup.procs; while :; do :; done' &
a=$(awk '/^usage_usec/{print $2}' capped/cpu.stat); sleep 10
b=$(awk '/^usage_usec/{print $2}' capped/cpu.stat)
echo "$(( (b - a) / 100000 ))% of one CPU"  # ~50 if enforced, ~100 if ignored
kill %1
blocks.caption: Not run here; run as root. usage_usec is reported in cpu.stat whether or not the cpu controller is enabled, so it measures what the task really got.

blocks.md: Measure percentiles, not means; A/B on one kernel, alternating runs, and report the spread. Then verify the nice and cgroup controls you depend on, because each scheduler decides which ones it honors.
Misconception: a lower average latency means a better scheduler. A policy can cut the median and still multiply the p99, and for interactive work the tail is what users feel.

blocks.question: Same machine, same schbench run. Scheduler X: wakeup p50 6 us, p99 2,100 us. Fair class: p50 9 us, p99 240 us. Requests per second are equal. For a service with a tail-latency target, what follows?
options: X is better: its median is a third lower
The fair class is better for the tail: X's p99 is almost 9 times higher
They are equal, because throughput is equal
Nothing: percentiles from different schedulers cannot be compared
blocks.explain: With equal throughput the deciding number for a tail-latency target is p99, and 2,100 us against 240 us is about 8.75 times worse. Comparing percentiles across schedulers on the same kernel, machine and workload is exactly what an A/B test is for.

blocks.question: After loading your scheduler, SCX_EV_SELECT_CPU_FALLBACK in /sys/kernel/sched_ext/root/events climbs steadily. What does it point to?
options: The scheduler keeps entering bypass mode
Tasks are being inserted without a slice
Your select_cpu returns CPUs the tasks cannot use, and the core silently picks another one
The watchdog is about to declare a stall
blocks.explain: The kernel docs define it as ops.select_cpu() returning a CPU unusable by the task, after which the core picks a fallback. Look for a missing check against p->cpus_ptr, the task's allowed cpumask.

blocks.question: Your cpu.max test shows a cgroup capped at 50 percent using 98 percent of a CPU under scx_flatcg. What is the right conclusion?
options: usage_usec is not counted for tasks on the ext class
cpu.max applies only to SCHED_DEADLINE tasks
The test is wrong: cpu.max is always enforced by the kernel core
scx_flatcg does not implement cgroup_set_bandwidth, so the cpu.max cap is ignored while it runs
blocks.explain: The kernel passes cpu.max to the BPF scheduler through ops.cgroup_set_bandwidth(), and each scheduler chooses whether to implement it. scx_flatcg implements cpu.weight only. usage_usec is always reported, which is why it works as a check.
